header: National Bank of Pakistan Versus M/s. Hussain Mills Limited
Order with Signature of Judge, and that of parties or
29.10.2026 Ms. Ambreen Moeen, ASC and Javeria Latif, Advocate for
the Decree Holder/National Bank of Pakistan.
Mr. Zohaib Hassan, Advocate for the Judgment Debtor.
body: Mian Babur Saleem, ASC/Court Auctioneer.

C.M. No.3634 of 2026 This is an Application under Section 19 of the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001 (the “Ordinance”) read with Section 151 CPC, seeking release of an amount of Rs.1,500,000/- from the Decree Holder/Bank towards the expenses to be incurred in connection with the auction proceedings.

2. Mian Babur Saleem, ASC/Court Auctioneer, submitted that vide order dated 15.09.2026, he was appointed to conduct the auction of several properties, including substantial structures erected thereon, as reflected in the Fard-e-Taliqa. He stated that an estimated amount of Rs.15,00,000/- is required towards valuation of the properties, publication of the sale proclamation in widely circulated Urdu and English daily newspapers, drum beating, posters, pana flexes, video/audio recording, notices, tenting/air-conditioning, transportation, labour and other miscellaneous expenses. He added that the item-wise details of the actual expenses would be furnished along with the auction report. He, therefore, urged that the Decree- Holder Bank be directed to release the aforesaid amount to facilitate timely completion of the auction proceedings.

3. Conversely, Ms. Ambreen Moeen, ASC, for the Decree Holder/Bank submitted on the basis of reply that the application filed by the Court Auctioneer seeking an advance amount of Rs.1,500,000/- towards anticipated auction expenses is premature, misconceived and devoid of lawful justification. She stated that the remuneration of the learned Court Auctioneer had already been fixed at Rs.150,000/- by this Court vide order dated 15.09.2026, whereas the fee for valuation of the properties had separately been fixed at Rs.450,000/- under the same order. She urged that the applicant could not claim the valuation charges again under the head of additional auction expenses or demand an advance of estimated expenditure as a matter of right before conducting the auction. She further submitted that Rule 22, Chapter 12, Part L, Volume I, of the Lahore High Court Rules and Orders (the “Rules and Orders”) governs the sale of property in execution of decrees and the role, appointment and duties of the Court Auctioneer. She urged that Rule 22(iv) expressly provides that where an auction sale is ordered but is not completed or does not take place, the Court Auctioneer shall be entitled only to his fee, the amount whereof is to be determined by the Court. In this regard, she relied upon the judgment of the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan in United Bank Limited v. C.M. Sarwar, Advocate and others (PLJ 2004 SC 213), wherein it was held that, under Rule 22 of the Rules and Orders, a Court Auctioneer is entitled only to actual expenses and not commission where the auction sale is not completed or finalized, as commission is deductible and payable strictly out of the completed sale proceeds upon confirmation.

4. Ms. Ambreen Moeen, ASC, added that the amount of Rs.1,500,000/- had been claimed under various heads, including newspaper publication, drum beating, posters, printing of pana flexes, video/audio recording, notices, tenting/air-conditioning, transportation, computer and printer expenses, electricity, stationery, labour and miscellaneous expenses, without establishing that any such expenditure had actually been incurred. She pointed out that the applicant had himself stated that details of the expenses would be furnished along with the auction report, which demonstrated that the present demand was based merely on anticipated expenditure. She urged that the applicant was required to conduct the auction proceedings and thereafter submit a duly itemised statement of actual expenses, supported by relevant invoices, receipts and other documentary evidence, for determination by this Court in accordance with law. Regarding newspaper publication charges, she submitted that under Order XXI, Rule 67(2)(i) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (the “CPC”), as applicable in Punjab, where the reserve price exceeds Rs.2,000,000/-, publication of the sale proclamation in at least one widely circulated national daily newspaper is required and the expenses incurred in such publication constitute costs of the sale. She stated that the Decree- Holder/Bank would itself arrange publication of the sale proclamation in both newspapers and seek reimbursement of the actual publication expenses, as admissible under law, upon successful completion of the auction, with such expenses being adjusted against the sale proceeds. Thus, the applicant could not include such charges in the advance without establishing their legal admissibility as expenses payable to him or the Bank's liability to pay them in advance. She further argued that Order XXI, Rules 65, 66 and 67 of CPC regulate the conduct of execution sales, preparation of the sale proclamation and its publication, but do not authorise the Court Auctioneer to demand an unverified advance amount towards anticipated expenditure. She added that neither the appointment order dated 15.09.2026 nor the applicable provisions conferred upon the applicant an unrestricted right to claim additional funds without establishing the legal basis, necessity and reasonableness of each item of expenditure. Lastly, she submitted that if the Court Auctioneer was unwilling to proceed on the aforesaid terms, he could be replaced by another suitable Court Auctioneer to ensure the smooth and expeditious completion of the auction proceedings.
5. Mr. Zohaib Hassan, Advocate appearing on behalf of the Judgment Debtor, has conceded with the arguments of learned counsel for the Decree Holder Bank.
6. Arguments heard. Record perused.

7. Perusal of the record reveals that, vide order dated 15.09.2026, this Court had appointed the applicant as Court Auctioneer and fixed his remuneration at Rs.150,000/-. Since M/s. Hussain Mills Limited (Company)/Judgment Debtor has various Units, therefore, this Court also appointed Evaluator for valuation of the properties and his fee was separately fixed as Rs.450,000/-. The applicant now seeks a further amount of Rs.1,500,000/- towards various expenses, including valuation, publication and other incidental expenses, before completion of the auction proceedings. Significantly, the applicant has himself stated that the details of the expenses would be furnished along with the auction report. Thus, the amount presently claimed is only an estimate of anticipated expenditure and is not supported by any itemised account, invoices, receipts or other material establishing that the claimed expenses have actually been incurred.
8. This case revolves around Rule 22 of the High Court Rules and Orders and for ready reference the same is reproduced as under:

22. Charges of Court Auctioneers.-- (i) No commission shall be paid on the proceeds of sales set aside for a material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale. The commission on the proceeds of a sale set aside for any other cause shall be paid by the person at whose instance and for whose benefit the sale is set aside and the Court Auctioneer shall be entitled to his share of such commission.

(ii) If a sale is set aside the purchase money shall be refunded in full to the Auction Purchaser unless it is set aside at his instance and for his benefit in which event the commission due under paragraph 21 shall be deducted from the sum to be refunded.

(iii) Where a sale is set aside after the commission has been paid to the Court Auctioneer, the Court shall recover it from him and shall refund it to the Auction Purchaser if he is entitled to the refund of the whole of the purchase money. In such cases the Government share of the commission shall also be refunded.

(iv) In cases in which auction sales are ordered, but not completed or do not take place at all, the Court auctioneer shall be paid only his actual expenses, provided that if there has been, in the opinion of the Court, clear negligence on the part of the auctioneer (e.g., failure to advertise, leading to absence of bidders) he will not be entitled to any compensation. The amount of actual expenses if held due under this rule will be determined by the Court and shall be paid by the decreeholder or the judgment-debtor as the Court may direct.

Keeping in view the circumstances of the case, it is important to mention here that Rule 22(iv) ibid specifically provides that where an auction sale is ordered but is not completed or does not take place, the Court Auctioneer shall be entitled only to his actual expenses, subject to determination by the Court. The Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan, in the judgment reported as United Bank Limited v. C.M. Sarwar, Advocate and others (2004 PLJ SC 213), has also explained the entitlement of a Court Auctioneer under the said Rules, holding that, in the absence of a completed and finalised auction sale, the entitlement is confined to actual expenses and does not extend to commission payable out of the sale proceeds. The underlying principle is that the Court Auctioneer's entitlement must be determined in accordance with the applicable Rules and on the basis of expenses actually incurred, rather than on the basis of an unsubstantiated estimate. For ready reference the relevant part of the judgment is reproduced as under:
“From the bare perusal of the relevant rules reproduced above, it is expressly clear that the situation, which is involved in this case, is fully met with by Rules 21 & 22 (ibid)

according to which the commission would become due on the completion of the auction. The auction could not be held to have been completed before it was approved or confirmed by the Court. This staged did not reach in this case for before the confirmation of the sale by the cxecuting Court, execution petition was dismissed as barred by time therefore, commission had not become due as such it could not be recovered as sale proceeds were not paid to the decree holder.

7. Direction made by the High Court through the impugned order for payment of commission to the Court Auctioneers by the appellant is not sustainable. This appeal is accepted order dated 13.7.1995 is hereby set aside with no orders as to costs.”

Further reliance is palced on the judgment of this Court reported as “Bank EQUITY LIMITED versus QAND GHAR LIMITED and others” (2005 CLD 711), wherein it has been held that under Rule 3.2 of the Corporate and Industrial Restructuring Corporation Rules, 2001, read with Rule 21, Chapter 12-L, Volume I of the High Court Rules and Orders, where the Corporate and Industrial Restructuring Corporation or its nominee was appointed as Court Auctioneer on its own application, the Corporation was not entitled to any separate fee as Court Auctioneer, having already received 2% of the gross recoveries for the services rendered. Accordingly, this Court disallowed the claim of 2% of the total recoveries as remuneration of the Court Auctioneer and directed that the said amount be paid to the secured creditors in the ratio already determined. The relevant paragraphs are re-produced as under: “5. C.M. No.427-B of 2002 was made by CIRC under section 6(5) of the Non-Performing Assets and Rehabilitation of Industrial Undertaking (Legal Proceeding) Ordinance, 2000, seeking replacement of the existing Court Auctioneers with the nominees of CIRC. Mr.

Adeel K. Bajwa, Advocate and Mr. Mujeeb Anwar, Advocate, were appointed Joint Court Auctioneers in place of Mian Muhammad Iqbal, vide order dated 24-6-2002. CIRC made another application (C.M. No.426-B of 2002)
for appointment of the nominees of CIRC as Court Auctioneers. Vide order dated 30-10- 2002, my learned brother Jawwad S. Khawaja, J., appointed Mr. Adil Nisar Khan and Mr.

Farid Alam as Court Auctioneers. Under section 6(5) of the Non-Performing Assets and Rehabilitation of Industrial Undertaking (Legal Proceedings) Ordinance, 2000, in cases transferred to High Court, in which a Liquidator or a Court Auctioneer or a Receiver has already been appointed, the Corporation may apply to the High Court for replacement of the existing Liquidator or a Court Auctioneer or a Receiver, as the case may be and "the High Court shall thereupon appoint the Chief Executive of the Corporation or his nominees in place of the Liquidator or Court Auctioneer or a Receiver as the case may be". Under section 10 of the aforementioned Legal Proceedings, Ordinance, 2000, procedure for execution of the decree has been laid down. Under section 10(5) of the said Ordinance, 2000, the sale of the collateral or any part thereof by the Corporation pursuant to subsection (3) shall be either by Public Auctioneer or inviting sealed tenders subject to the orders of confirmation by the High Court. Under section 25(2) of the Corporate and Industrial Restructuring Corporation Ordinance, 2000, corporation fund consists of among others the recovery fee collected by the Corporation from financial institutions (in the instant case UBL). Under Rule 3.2 of the Corporate and Industrial Restructuring Corporation Rules, 2001, corporation is entitled to recover a fee equal to two per cent of the gross recoveries as compensation for its services.

6. In my view, where the CIRC or its nominee is appointed as Court Auctioneer on its own application, it is not entitled to any fee as Court Auctioneer. It has already received 2% of the gross recoveries for the services rendered. In the circumstances, 2 per cent of the total recoveries as Court Auctioneer's remunerations are disallowed. The Court Auctioneers are further directed to make the payment of the said amount to the secured creditors in the ratio already determined. ...”

9. Furthermore, the remuneration of the applicant and the valuation fee having already been fixed by this Court, any further claim under these heads must be supported by a distinct and lawful basis and cannot result in duplication of the amounts already determined. Likewise, although Order XXI, Rules 65, 66 and 67 CPC provide the legal framework for conducting an execution sale and publishing the sale proclamation, these provisions do not, by themselves, establish an automatic entitlement in favour of the Court Auctioneer to receive an advance of Rs.1,500,000/- without furnishing particulars and supporting material. The mere filing of an affidavit does not establish the actual incurrence, necessity or reasonableness of the expenditure claimed.

10. In these circumstances, the applicant has failed to establish any presently enforceable entitlement to the advance amount sought. This, however, shall not preclude him from submitting, upon completion of the relevant auction-related work, an itemised statement of actual and necessary expenses, supported by documentary evidence, for determination by this Court in accordance with Rule 22(iv) of the Rules and Orders. Any claim relating to publication charges shall likewise be considered in accordance with Order XXI, Rule 67 CPC and the applicable law. The applicant shall remain bound by the terms of his appointment order dated 15.09.2026.
11. Consequently, the instant application, being premature and unsupported by proof of actual expenditure, is dismissed.
Main Case 12. Re-list on 26.11.2026.
